entries.subject: Observatory photographs of the Sombrero Galaxy
entries.finding: Not surveyed: the Messier galaxies of this batch share one survey so that they match. An observatory photograph with sky coordinates would show more detail.
entries.revisitWhen: A whole-galaxy photograph with sky coordinates is published under an attribution licence.

entries.subject: Stars in the picture
entries.finding: The picture was first cleaned only by the bake's pass over the Gaia foreground stars, which leaves the brightest stars, the faint ones Gaia cannot certify and those it reads as extended. The Nebula Lab's NOX removes them all and keeps the galaxy's arms and dust lanes; it also takes the galaxy's own compact knots and clusters, most visibly in M51, which was looked at and accepted on 2026-10-03; 6 of the 6 Gaia stars brighter than G 14 in the picture had a glow, filled out to at most 230 px (62″). The lab's isophote fill, made for ellipticals, left a dark notch on a spiral, so the glow is filled from the ring around it.

entries.subject: Catalogued objects as dots
entries.finding: 948 dots from 2 published tables: 659 globular clusters (Spitler et al. (2006), CDS J/AJ/132/1593, 659 rows in the file); 289 planetary nebulae (Ford et al. (1996), CDS J/ApJ/458/455, 294 rows in the file). Each dot is a catalogued object at its published sky position, placed on the plane the picture stands on; its depth is not measured, and it is not drawn.

entries.subject: Bulge
entries.finding: Salo et al. (2015), S4G Pipeline 4, table 7, NGC4594, model _bz: a Sérsic bulge (82.6% of the light, magnitude 7.317, half-light radius 180.42″ = 8.21 kpc, n = 4.663, axis ratio 0.608, PA 88.81°) and an edge-on disc (17.4% of the light, scale length 49.25″ = 2.24 kpc, scale height 10.80″ = 0.49 kpc, PA 89.25°, central surface brightness 17.946 as seen). Used as published; the half-light surface brightness the bake needs, 21.527 mag per square arcsecond, follows from the bulge's magnitude, radius, index and axis ratio. The picture faces the Sun, so the spheroid takes the galaxy's own disc: S4G fits this galaxy's disc with its edge-on disc function (component Z, edgedisk), the profile of a disc seen at 90°, at this position angle. At that tilt the bulge's axis ratio is one an oblate spheroid in the disc plane can show (intrinsic 0.61).
